name: Granada
tagline: The Alhambra, the Albaicín and free tapas
summary: The last Moorish kingdom in Spain, under the Sierra Nevada. Book the Alhambra first, then spend the rest of the time in the hillside lanes of the Albaicín, the cave quarter of Sacromonte and the tapas bars, where a free plate comes with every drink.
seasonNote: July and August pass 38°C; winter is cold at night but clear, with snow on the mountains behind the Alhambra.
arrival: Fast trains from Madrid take about 3 hours 20 minutes; buses from Málaga airport take 1 hour 40 minutes. Granada's small airport has a bus to the cathedral.
gettingAround: The centre is walkable but steep; small C1, C2 and C3 minibuses climb to the Albaicín, Sacromonte and the Alhambra.
cashTip: Cards are accepted almost everywhere; carry coins for the minibuses if you have no card.
foodTip: Order a drink and a tapa arrives free; try remojón salad, habas con jamón and piononos pastries from Santa Fe.
buyTip: Inlaid wooden boxes (taracea), Fajalauza ceramics and lanterns in the Alcaicería market.
baseArea: Near Plaza Nueva, between the cathedral, the Albaicín and the Alhambra

connections.note: Trains via Antequera; buses take about 3 hours.

items.name: Alhambra
items.summary: A Nasrid palace-city of carved stucco, tiled halls and courtyard pools, with the Generalife gardens beside it.
items.expect: Tickets sell out weeks ahead and the Nasrid Palaces entry is at a fixed half-hour; bring your passport.
items.tip: Book on the official site only, take the earliest Nasrid slot, and see the Alcazaba and gardens around it.
items.why: The finest Islamic palace in Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Minibus C3 or walk up through the woods from Plaza Nueva.
Alcazaba, Nasrid Palaces at your slot, then the Generalife.

items.name: Mirador de San Nicolás
items.summary: The square in front of a church with the classic view of the Alhambra against the Sierra Nevada.
items.expect: Packed at sunset with musicians and vendors; watch bags.
items.tip: For a quieter version walk five minutes up to the Mirador de San Cristóbal or Mirador de la Vereda de Enmedio.
items.why: The most famous view in Spain.
flow: Minibus C1 or climb through the Albaicín.
Stay for the sunset, then tapas on the way down.

items.name: Albaicín
items.summary: The old Moorish quarter of whitewashed houses, walled gardens (carmenes) and cobbled lanes facing the Alhambra.
items.expect: Steep and confusing; that is half the pleasure.
items.tip: Walk up Carrera del Darro along the river and get lost on purpose, ending at San Nicolás.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site along with the Alhambra.
flow: Start at Plaza Nueva.
Carrera del Darro, El Bañuelo baths, then up the lanes.

items.name: Sacromonte caves
items.summary: A hillside of cave homes where the Roma community developed its own flamenco, the zambra.
items.expect: Evening flamenco in the caves is intimate and touristy in equal measure.
items.tip: Visit the Cuevas del Sacromonte museum by day, and book a show at a small cave venue.
items.why: The most atmospheric place to see flamenco in Andalusia.
flow: Minibus C2 from Plaza Nueva.
Cave museum, then return for an evening show.

items.name: Royal Chapel and Cathedral
items.summary: The tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella, the monarchs who took Granada in 1492, beside a vast Renaissance cathedral.
items.expect: Two separate tickets; photos are not allowed in the chapel crypt.
items.tip: See the chapel first: Isabella's own art collection is in the sacristy.
items.why: The end of Moorish Spain and the start of the Spanish empire in one room.
flow: Walk from Plaza Nueva.
Royal Chapel, then the cathedral, then the Alcaicería market.

items.name: Monastery of San Jerónimo
items.summary: A Renaissance monastery with an orange-tree cloister and a painted church interior.
items.expect: Rarely busy; still home to an order of nuns.
items.tip: A short walk from the cathedral; go at midday when other sights are full.
items.why: One of the most richly decorated churches in Spain, with few visitors.
flow: Walk 10 minutes north-west of the cathedral.
Cloister, then the church.

items.name: Bar Los Diamantes
items.summary: A standing-room bar famous for fried fish tapas.
items.expect: Crowded and loud; order at the bar.
items.tip: Each drink brings a free tapa; order a ración of the fried mix to share.
items.why: The best-known tapas bar in Granada.
flow: Squeeze to the counter.
Beer, free tapa, then a plate of fried fish.

items.name: Bodegas Castañeda
items.summary: An old wine bar with barrels behind the counter and hams hanging above.
items.expect: Busy from 8 pm.
items.tip: Ask for a vermouth from the barrel.
items.why: A classic Granada bar for cured meat and cheese.
flow: Near Plaza Nueva.
Drinks with free tapas, then a cheese board.

items.name: Calle Calderería Nueva tea houses
items.summary: A narrow lane of Moroccan-style tea houses, bakeries and shawarma shops at the foot of the Albaicín.
items.expect: Low cushioned seating and dozens of teas.
items.tip: Stop here halfway up to San Nicolás.
items.why: Granada's Moorish past in a cup.
flow: Off Calle Elvira.
Mint tea and pastries, then on up the hill.

name: Valencia
tagline: Paella, futuristic architecture and a city beach
summary: Spain's third city combines a well-kept old town, the white buildings of the City of Arts and Sciences and a long beach, all linked by a park in the old riverbed. It is also the home of paella.
seasonNote: Las Fallas in mid-March fills the streets with giant figures and fireworks, and hotel prices triple; August is humid.
arrival: High-speed trains from Madrid take 1 hour 45 minutes, from Barcelona about 3 hours. Metro lines 3 and 5 reach the airport in 20 minutes.
gettingAround: The old town is walkable; cycle the Turia park; metro and tram to the beach.
foodTip: Real paella valenciana has rabbit, chicken and beans; eat it at lunch, not dinner. Try horchata with fartons and arroz negro.
buyTip: Lladró porcelain, fans and ceramics from Manises; saffron and rice from the Central Market.
baseArea: Ciutat Vella (old town) or Ruzafa for restaurants

items.name: City of Arts and Sciences
items.summary: Santiago Calatrava's complex of white futuristic buildings over shallow pools: science museum, opera house and Europe's largest aquarium.
items.expect: The outside is free; each building has its own ticket.
items.tip: Choose the Oceanogràfic if you only do one, and come back after dark when it is lit.
items.why: The defining image of modern Valencia.
flow: Walk or cycle down the Turia park.
Walk around the pools, then the Oceanogràfic.

items.name: Mercado Central
items.summary: One of Europe's largest fresh markets, under a modernist dome of iron, glass and tiles.
items.expect: Open mornings Monday to Saturday.
items.tip: Have breakfast at Central Bar inside the market.
items.why: The building and the produce are both worth the visit.
flow: Arrive by 10 am.
Walk every aisle, then the Lonja opposite.

items.name: La Lonja de la Seda
items.summary: A 15th-century silk exchange with twisted stone columns rising like palm trees.
items.expect: Small and free on Sundays.
items.tip: Look at the carved gargoyles on the outside.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and a Gothic masterpiece.
flow: Opposite the Central Market.
Trading hall, orange-tree courtyard, upper hall.

items.name: Valencia Cathedral and the Micalet tower
items.summary: A cathedral that claims the Holy Grail, with a bell tower climb over the old town.
items.expect: 207 spiral steps up the tower.
items.tip: On Thursdays at noon the 1,000-year-old Water Tribunal meets at the Door of the Apostles.
items.why: The heart of the old city and its best viewpoint.
flow: Plaza de la Reina.
Grail chapel, then the Micalet.

items.name: Turia Gardens
items.summary: A 9 km park in the dry bed of the diverted river, with paths, bridges and playgrounds.
items.expect: Flat and shaded; bike rental at many points.
items.tip: Cycle from the Torres de Serranos to the City of Arts and Sciences.
items.why: The way locals move through the city.
flow: Hire a bike near the Serranos towers.
Ride south-east to the Calatrava buildings.

items.name: Malvarrosa Beach and El Cabanyal
items.summary: A wide city beach beside an old fishermen's quarter of tiled houses.
items.expect: Busy in summer; restaurants line the promenade.
items.tip: Eat paella on the seafront at lunch and walk the tiled streets of El Cabanyal.
items.why: A real beach 20 minutes from the cathedral.
flow: Tram or metro to the beach.
Swim, lunch, walk back through El Cabanyal.

items.name: Albufera Natural Park
items.summary: A freshwater lagoon among rice fields where paella was born; boats take you out at sunset.
items.expect: A 30-minute bus ride; mosquitoes in summer.
items.tip: Take the boat in El Palmar at sunset, then eat paella in the village.
items.why: The landscape behind the dish.
flow: Bus 25 from the centre.
Boat on the lagoon, then dinner in El Palmar.

items.name: Casa Carmela
items.summary: A family restaurant cooking paella over orange-wood fires since 1922.
items.expect: Lunch only; paella for two or more.
items.tip: Reserve and pre-order the paella valenciana.
items.why: Often called the best paella in Valencia.
flow: Book ahead.
Starters, then the paella pan to share.

items.name: Horchatería Santa Catalina
items.summary: A tiled 200-year-old café serving horchata, the cold drink made from tiger nuts.
items.expect: Busy in the afternoon.
items.tip: Dip fartons, long sugared buns, into the horchata.
items.why: The classic Valencian afternoon treat.
flow: Next to the church of Santa Catalina.
Horchata and fartons.

items.name: Central Bar
items.summary: Chef Ricard Camarena's counter inside the Central Market, serving sandwiches and tapas from market produce.
items.expect: Stools only; no reservations.
items.tip: Order the esmorzaret, Valencia's mid-morning sandwich break.
items.why: A Michelin-starred chef's food at bar prices.
flow: Inside the market.
Wait for a stool, then sandwiches and a beer.

name: Málaga · Costa del Sol
tagline: Picasso's city, a Moorish fortress and the beach
summary: The gateway to the Costa del Sol has become a city of museums, with a Moorish fortress above the port and a city beach. It is the best base for Ronda, the Caminito del Rey and the white villages.
seasonNote: Over 300 days of sun; winters are mild enough for lunch outdoors. Holy Week processions in spring are among Spain's biggest.
arrival: The airport is 8 km away; the C1 train reaches the centre in 12 minutes. High-speed trains from Madrid take 2 hours 40 minutes.
gettingAround: The centre is walkable; buses and the coast train serve the beaches. Ronda and the Caminito need a bus, train or car.
foodTip: Espetos (sardines grilled on skewers over a beach fire), pescaíto frito, ajoblanco cold soup and sweet Málaga wine.
buyTip: Sweet Málaga wine, olive oil and ceramics.
baseArea: The historic centre near Calle Larios

connections.note: Trains via Córdoba or buses in 2 hours 45 minutes.

items.name: Alcazaba and Gibralfaro
items.summary: An 11th-century Moorish palace-fortress with courtyards and fountains, and a castle above it with views over the bay.
items.expect: Steep walk to Gibralfaro; bus 35 goes up.
items.tip: Take the bus up to Gibralfaro and walk down through the Alcazaba; free on Sunday afternoons.
items.why: The best Moorish monument on the coast.
flow: Bus 35 to Gibralfaro.
Castle walls, then down to the Alcazaba and the Roman theatre.

items.name: Museo Picasso Málaga
items.summary: More than 200 works by Picasso in a Renaissance palace near the house where he was born.
items.expect: Busy at midday; free in the last two hours on Sunday.
items.tip: Pair with the Casa Natal, his birthplace, five minutes away.
items.why: The artist's home town honours him with a strong collection.
flow: Calle San Agustín.
Collection, then the Phoenician ruins in the basement.

items.name: Málaga Cathedral
items.summary: A Renaissance cathedral nicknamed La Manquita, 'the one-armed lady', because one tower was never finished.
items.expect: Rooftop tours run at set times.
items.tip: Book the rooftop walk for a view down on the old town.
items.why: The landmark of the centre.
flow: Walk from Calle Larios.
Nave, choir stalls, then the roof.

items.name: Muelle Uno and La Malagueta beach
items.summary: A palm-lined port promenade with the Pompidou cube, leading to the city beach.
items.expect: Restaurants and beach bars along the sand.
items.tip: Walk the port at sunset and eat espetos on the beach.
items.why: Málaga's waterfront in one easy walk.
flow: Start at Palmeral de las Sorpresas.
Muelle Uno, the lighthouse, La Malagueta.

items.name: Caminito del Rey
items.summary: A walkway bolted to the sides of a gorge 100 metres above the river.
items.expect: Timed tickets, a helmet, 8 km of walking one way and no children under eight.
items.tip: Book weeks ahead and take the train to El Chorro.
items.why: One of Europe's most thrilling walks, now safe.
flow: Train or bus to El Chorro.
Shuttle to the north entrance, walk the gorge south.

items.name: Ronda
items.summary: A white town split by a 100-metre gorge and joined by the Puente Nuevo bridge.
items.expect: Two hours by bus or train; crowded with day tours at midday.
items.tip: Stay overnight to see the bridge lit and empty.
items.why: The most dramatic town in Andalusia.
flow: Bus or train from Málaga.
Puente Nuevo, the bullring, then down the path below the bridge.

items.name: Nerja and Frigiliana
items.summary: A seaside town with the Balcón de Europa viewpoint and huge caves, below the white hill village of Frigiliana.
items.expect: An hour east by bus.
items.tip: Frigiliana first in the morning, then a swim and lunch in Nerja.
items.why: The prettiest part of the coast near Málaga.
flow: Bus to Nerja, then a short bus up to Frigiliana.
Village lanes, then the Balcón de Europa.

items.name: Mercado de Atarazanas
items.summary: A covered market behind a Moorish gate, with tapas bars cooking fish from the stalls.
items.expect: Mornings only; closed Sunday.
items.tip: Eat fried fish at the bars along the seafood aisle.
items.why: The city's freshest food at market prices.
flow: Walk from Calle Larios.
Browse, then sit at a bar for fried fish.

items.name: El Pimpi
items.summary: A rambling bodega of patios and rooms with barrels signed by famous visitors, beside the Roman theatre.
items.expect: Touristy and very popular.
items.tip: Take a terrace table facing the Alcazaba and order sweet wine.
items.why: The most famous bar in Málaga, with the best setting.
flow: Calle Granada.
Sweet wine and tapas on the terrace.

items.name: El Tintero
items.summary: A beach restaurant where waiters walk among tables shouting the dishes and you grab what you want.
items.expect: Chaotic and fun; pay by counting plates.
items.tip: Grab espetos of sardines straight off the fire.
items.why: A uniquely Málaga way of eating seafood.
flow: Bus to El Palo beach.
Grab plates as they pass.

name: San Sebastián · Basque Country
tagline: Pintxos bars and a perfect bay
summary: An elegant resort on a shell-shaped bay with one of the world's greatest concentrations of good food, from pintxos counters to famous tasting menus. Bilbao and its Guggenheim are an hour away.
seasonNote: Rain is possible all year and common from November to April; summer is mild and busy.
arrival: Fly to Bilbao (an hour by bus) or San Sebastián's small airport; trains from Madrid take about 5 hours. Biarritz in France is 45 minutes away.
gettingAround: Walk everything; local buses and the Euskotren to Bilbao and France.
cashTip: Pintxos bars accept cards but cash is quicker at a busy counter.
foodTip: Do a txikiteo: one pintxo and a small drink per bar, then move on. Order the hot pintxos from the board, not just what sits on the counter.
buyTip: Txakoli wine, Idiazabal cheese and Basque linen.
baseArea: Parte Vieja (old town) for the bars; Centro or Gros for quieter nights

connections.note: Direct trains; flights take an hour from Bilbao or San Sebastián.
Via Hendaye on the French border.

items.name: La Concha Beach
items.summary: A curving city beach with a white railing promenade, often called the most beautiful urban beach in Europe.
items.expect: Calm water and a lifeguarded swim season from June to September.
items.tip: Walk the promenade from the town hall to Ondarreta at low tide.
items.why: The image of the city.
flow: Start at the town hall gardens.
Walk the bay to Peine del Viento.

items.name: Parte Vieja pintxos crawl
items.summary: The old town's lanes hold dozens of bars with counters covered in small bites.
items.expect: Packed from 8 pm; stand at the bar.
items.tip: Pick three or four bars and order one speciality at each.
items.why: This is what people travel to San Sebastián for.
flow: Start on Calle 31 de Agosto.
Move bar to bar, ending at Plaza de la Constitución.

items.name: Monte Igueldo
items.summary: A hill at the end of the bay reached by a 1912 funicular, with an old-fashioned amusement park on top.
items.expect: Small fee for the funicular.
items.tip: Go up at sunset for the view over the whole bay and Santa Clara island.
items.why: The classic photo of La Concha.
flow: Walk to the end of Ondarreta beach.
Funicular up, then the lookout.

items.name: Monte Urgull
items.summary: A wooded hill above the old town with castle ruins and a statue of Christ.
items.expect: A 20-minute climb on shaded paths; free.
items.tip: Walk up from the port and down to the aquarium.
items.why: A quieter view over both beaches and the old town.
flow: Start at the harbour.
Climb to the Mota castle.

items.name: San Telmo Museum
items.summary: A museum of Basque society in a 16th-century convent with a modern wing.
items.expect: Closed on Mondays.
items.tip: See the painted chapel by Josep Maria Sert.
items.why: The best introduction to Basque identity.
flow: Edge of the old town.
Cloister, chapel, then the history rooms.

items.name: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
items.summary: Frank Gehry's titanium museum on the river, with Jeff Koons's flower Puppy at the door.
items.expect: An hour each way by bus; closed some Mondays.
items.tip: Book online and eat pintxos in Bilbao's old town afterwards.
items.why: The building that changed museum architecture.
flow: Bus from San Sebastián to Bilbao.
Museum, then the Casco Viejo.

items.name: Gandarias
items.summary: A busy bar known for its sirloin pintxo and a long counter of cold bites.
items.expect: Crowded; pushing to the counter is normal.
items.tip: Order the solomillo from the kitchen.
items.why: A reliable first stop on any crawl.
flow: Calle 31 de Agosto.
Sirloin pintxo and a txakoli.

items.name: La Viña
items.summary: The bar that invented the burnt Basque cheesecake now copied around the world.
items.expect: A queue for slices; cakes are lined up on the counter.
items.tip: Order a slice with a glass of sweet wine.
items.why: The original of a global trend.
flow: Calle 31 de Agosto.
Cheesecake to finish the crawl.

items.name: Bar Nestor
items.summary: A tiny bar with a short menu: tomato salad, steak by the kilo, and a Spanish omelette made twice a day.
items.expect: Tortilla is cut at 1 pm and 8 pm; put your name down well before.
items.tip: Arrive half an hour early to reserve a slice of tortilla.
items.why: A cult favourite of chefs and locals.
flow: Calle Pescadería.
Sign up for tortilla, then steak and peppers.

name: Palma · Mallorca
tagline: Gothic cathedral, mountain villages and turquoise coves
summary: Mallorca's capital has a beautiful old town and a cathedral on the sea wall. Beyond it are the Tramuntana mountains, stone villages like Deià and Valldemossa, and the cove beaches of the east coast.
seasonNote: July and August are very busy and expensive; many resorts close from November to March but Palma stays open.
arrival: Palma airport is 8 km away; bus A1 reaches the centre in 20 minutes. Ferries run from Barcelona and Valencia.
gettingAround: Walk old Palma. TIB buses and the vintage train to Sóller cover the island; a car is easiest for coves.
foodTip: Ensaïmada pastry for breakfast, pa amb oli with tomato and cured meat, sobrassada sausage and tumbet vegetables.
buyTip: Ensaïmadas in a box for the plane, olive wood, and leather shoes from Inca.
baseArea: The old town (Casco Antiguo) or Santa Catalina for restaurants

items.name: Palma Cathedral (La Seu)
items.summary: A Gothic cathedral on the sea wall with one of the largest rose windows in the world and a canopy by Gaudí.
items.expect: Closed to visits on Sundays except for Mass.
items.tip: Visit mid-morning for the coloured light from the rose window.
items.why: The landmark of Mallorca.
flow: Walk along the sea wall.
Nave, Gaudí's canopy, Barceló's chapel.

items.name: Palma old town and Arab Baths
items.summary: Lanes of honey-coloured mansions with hidden patios, and 10th-century Moorish baths.
items.expect: Quiet streets behind the cathedral.
items.tip: Peer into the patios on Carrer de la Almudaina and Carrer de Sant Miquel.
items.why: Palma is much more than a beach airport.
flow: Behind the cathedral.
Arab Baths, then the patios and Plaça Major.

items.name: Bellver Castle
items.summary: A rare round Gothic castle on a wooded hill over the bay.
items.expect: Closed on Mondays; a steep climb or a short taxi.
items.tip: Free on Sundays.
items.why: The best view of Palma and its harbour.
flow: Bus or taxi up the hill.
Roof walk, then down through the pine woods.

items.name: Sóller train and Port de Sóller
items.summary: A 1912 wooden train through the mountains to Sóller, then a vintage tram to the harbour.
items.expect: Expensive and busy; the bus is faster and cheaper.
items.tip: Train one way, bus back over the mountains.
items.why: The most scenic ride on the island.
flow: Train from Plaça d'Espanya.
Sóller square, tram to the port, swim, bus back.

items.name: Valldemossa and Deià
items.summary: Stone villages in the Tramuntana mountains, a UNESCO landscape; Chopin wintered in Valldemossa's monastery.
items.expect: Narrow mountain roads; tour buses fill Valldemossa at midday.
items.tip: Arrive early, have a coca de patata bun, then go on to Deià and its cove.
items.why: The mountain side of Mallorca that many beach visitors miss.
flow: Bus 203 from Palma.
Valldemossa monastery, then Deià and Cala Deià.

items.name: Caló des Moro
items.summary: A tiny cove of turquoise water between pine-covered cliffs, the most photographed beach on the island.
items.expect: Very small, no facilities, a steep rocky path and huge summer crowds.
items.tip: Go at 8 am or late afternoon, or swim at Cala S'Almunia next door.
items.why: The Mallorca of the postcards.
flow: Drive about an hour south-east.
Walk down to the cove, then on to Cala Llombards.

items.name: Cap de Formentor
items.summary: A narrow headland of cliffs and a lighthouse at the island's northern tip.
items.expect: The road is closed to private cars in peak summer; take the shuttle bus.
items.tip: Stop at the Mirador Es Colomer viewpoint on the way.
items.why: The most dramatic scenery on Mallorca.
flow: Drive or bus to Port de Pollença.
Viewpoint, Formentor beach, then the lighthouse.

items.name: Mercat de l'Olivar
items.summary: Palma's main food market with tapas bars and oyster counters among the stalls.
items.expect: Closed Sunday; busiest on Saturday mornings.
items.tip: Eat sushi or oysters at the fish hall counters.
items.why: Where locals shop and lunch.
flow: Walk from Plaça d'Espanya.
Browse, then sit at a counter.

items.name: Ca'n Joan de s'Aigo
items.summary: A tiled café open since 1700, famous for ensaïmadas and almond ice cream.
items.expect: A short queue at weekends.
items.tip: Order an ensaïmada with hot chocolate.
items.why: The classic Mallorcan breakfast in its best setting.
flow: Carrer de Can Sanç.
Ensaïmada and chocolate.

items.name: Santa Catalina restaurants
items.summary: A former fishermen's quarter that now holds Palma's densest cluster of good restaurants around its market.
items.expect: Lively until late, with tapas, Mallorcan and international food.
items.tip: Start at the market bars and wander Carrer de la Fàbrica.
items.why: The easiest place in Palma to find a good dinner without booking.
flow: Walk west from the old town.
Market bars, then dinner on Carrer de la Fàbrica.
